zh: 对单个商品来说，最后一次单点赋值会抹掉它之前的一切历史（初始价、更早的赋值、更早的全局下限）；之后只剩若干次全局“取 max”，而连续对多个阈值取 max 等于对其中最大的阈值取 max。注意 type 2 查询的第三列只是占位，阈值是第二列。
倒着扫描查询，维护目前遇到过的全局阈值最大值 floor（初始 0）。对每个商品，逆序中第一次遇到的单点赋值就是它正序的最后一次赋值，最终价格为 max(赋值, floor)，此时 floor 恰好是这次赋值之后所有全局阈值的最大值；之后再遇到它的单点赋值一律忽略。扫描结束后，从未被赋值的商品取 max(初始价, floor)。
读入价格数组和全部查询；准备 done 标记数组，floor=0。从最后一条查询往前：若类型为 2，floor=max(floor, 第二列)；若类型为 1 且商品 x（1-based）未完成，则令其价格为 max(v, floor) 并标记完成。最后遍历所有商品，未完成的价格改为 max(原价, floor)，按原顺序空格分隔输出。整体 O(n+q)。
en: For a single item, its last point assignment wipes out its entire earlier history (the initial price, earlier assignments and earlier global floors); after it only some global "take max" operations remain, and taking the max with several thresholds in a row equals taking the max with the largest of them. Note that the third column of a type 2 query is only a placeholder; the threshold is the second column.

Scan the queries backwards while keeping floor, the maximum global threshold seen so far (initially 0). For each item, the first point assignment met in reverse is its last assignment in forward order, and its final price is max(assigned value, floor), where floor is then exactly the largest global threshold after that assignment; any later-met assignments to that item are ignored. When the scan ends, every item that was never assigned gets max(initial price, floor).

Read the price array and all queries; keep a done array and floor=0. Going from the last query to the first: for type 2, set floor=max(floor, second column); for type 1, if item x (1-based) is not done yet, set its price to max(v, floor) and mark it done. Finally, go over all items, replace the price of each item that is not done with max(original price, floor), and print the prices in the original order separated by spaces. The whole thing is O(n+q).

explanationEn:
## Original source, full ranges and protocol adaptation

OA LIST/WeRide_OA/001, 005 and 006 at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc give getFinalPrice: operation 1 x v sets the price of item x directly to v, which may lower the price; operation 2 v r raises every price below v to v, which is equivalent to taking max(price,v) for every price. Operations are executed in input order.

The full constraints in 005: 1≤n,q≤200000, 0≤price[i],v≤1000000000, 1≤x≤n. The range must not be narrowed using this site's 100000/positive bounds from a similar problem. Every query always has three columns; 001 writes type2 as 2 v v, 005 explicitly writes 2 v r, and the explanation in 006 also contains 2 11 1. So the second column is the threshold and the third column takes no part in the defined global operation; we cannot additionally require the third column to equal the second. The original function takes int queries[q][3] and gives no range for the r column; this site explicitly interprets this placeholder field as a Java int, −2147483648..2147483647, and ignores it, without claiming that the original problem lists this decimal constraint.

This site's standard input is explicitly arranged as: n, one line of n prices, q, and q lines of three-integer queries. The original arrays and query parameters are kept; metadata such as the fixed column count 3 in the OCR layout is omitted, and the broken STDIN table is not treated as new queries. Indices are 1-based.

Public example 1 keeps [7,5,4] and the three queries from 001, with output [8,9,8]. Public example 2 keeps the five queries of 006 Sample0: the first step changes the third item from 3 to 4, the second step changes the last item from 5 to 1, and after the third step, a global floor of 3, the array should be [3,3,4,4,3]; then point 1 is set to 1 and point 2 is set to 2, giving the final [1,2,4,4,3]. The third item of the original output, written as 3, is wrong, and the original intermediate steps also miss or miswrite updates; this site corrects them according to the explicitly defined operations rather than changing the input to fit the wrong example. Public example 3 uses the actual STDIN of 006 Sample1, 2 8 8 and 2 11 11, and the output is four 11s, unchanged; the explanation writes 2 11 1 instead, which is inconsistent with the STDIN, but since the third column has no effect, both must give four 11s, and the last item must never stay at 1. A hidden case additionally covers this different placeholder.

## Approach

Scan the queries from back to front, maintaining floor, the maximum of all global raising thresholds encountered so far. For each item, only process the first point assignment met in reverse order; it is the last point assignment in forward order, and the final price is max(that assignment, floor). Earlier point assignments are ignored. After the whole scan, every item that was never assigned takes max(initial price, floor).

## Proof of correctness

For a fixed item, if it has point assignments, the last assignment in forward order overwrites every earlier state of the item, so the initial price, the other point assignments and the earlier global operations no longer affect it. After that last assignment only global raises remain; taking the max with several thresholds in turn equals taking the max with the largest of them. When the reverse scan meets that last assignment, floor contains exactly the global thresholds after it, which gives the correct final value; ignoring earlier operations once the item is marked done is also correct.

If an item is never point-assigned, its initial value only goes through global maxes. The floor at the end of the reverse scan contains all global thresholds, and taking the max with the initial value gives the final result. Every item falls into exactly one of these two cases, so the output array is correct. The initial floor=0 is valid because prices and valid thresholds are all non-negative; the third placeholder field takes no part in floor at all.

## Complexity

The reference runs in O(n+q) time and O(n+q) space for the prices, the done marks and the original query array, without recursion. All valid prices always lie in 0..1000000000 and fit in 32 bits; the third column is parsed through a 64-bit intermediate to avoid overflow when parsing the absolute value of INT_MIN, then stored in the original int field. Under the full n/q ranges memory stays far below 256MiB; the package allows 3 seconds and 64MiB of output to hold 200000 results.

## Independent verification

The small oracle executes queries one by one in forward order: a point assignment changes the array directly, and type2 scans all prices and takes the max. It does not reuse the reverse algorithm. The reference is actually run on 163 unique small cases, and forward states are additionally enumerated exhaustively for n=1..2, initial values 0..2 and up to 3 queries, cross-checked against an independent lazy-tag tree.

The large-scale oracle also works in forward order, using a binary tree with only a global-floor lazy tag: a global raise updates only the root tag; before a point assignment the ancestor tags along the path are pushed down, then the leaf is overwritten, and finally the tags are propagated downward to read all leaf values. This differs from the reference's reverse last-assignment/suffix-maximum implementation. Full n=q=200000 cases cover global raises, assigning every point, repeatedly overwriting the same point, a global 1e9 followed by assigning 0 at the end, no point assignments, random values over the full range, and INT_MIN/INT_MAX placeholders; structured data are additionally checked in closed form. Three negative controls respectively misuse the placeholder as the threshold, take an earlier point assignment, and wrongly apply a past global floor to a later lower price; each counts as killed only if it exits normally on all official cases.
